strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly formalizes exploration stagnation and its practical significance with mathematical justification (zero gradients for none-pass samples)
Practical approach without external guidance: exploits only model's own trials, avoiding requirements for human annotations or stronger LLMs

Comprehensive empirical analysis for 4B model: substantial improvements (+6.38 Pass@1, +9.00 Pass@k), thorough investigation of training dynamics, and clear demonstration that LTE reduces none-pass samples while maintaining learning signal
Strong analysis of exploration-exploitation tradeoff: Figure 4 effectively shows LTE maintains higher entropy and increases response length, confirming improved internal exploration capability
Clear presentation with effective visualizations: well-structured paper with informative figures and readable prose throughout
Theoretical grounding: provides formal state space pruning analysis and information-theoretic justification in appendices
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core idea of using incorrect answers as negative hints is straightforward; mixed-policy optimization closely follows Yan et al. (2025). Combines existing techniques rather than introducing fundamentally new insights

Inconsistent results on 8B model: Table 1 shows minimal improvements for larger model (+1.00 Pass@k without entropy loss, variable Pass@1 gains). Attribution to 'small training data' lacks rigorous investigation, raising robustness concerns

Very limited training scale: only 9,189 and 3,236 training samples (Table 2) make generalization to realistic settings uncertain. Short 300-step training with batch size 128 insufficient to establish convergence properties

Incomplete experimental evaluation: missing direct empirical comparison with EvoCoT (similar self-contained approach), no comprehensive ablations on hint types or design choices, no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals

Weak theoretical analysis: assumption that α ∼ Ω(1) is unjustified; information gain result (Eq. 25) is tautological; approximations only valid in limited regimes. Theory provides limited insight beyond intuition
Unjustified method design choices: unclear why to randomly replace G′ responses vs. using all correct solutions, why treat truncated responses as void, why set γ=0.1 and approximate π_old as 1

Narrow scope: only evaluated on mathematics with concise extractable answers. Authors acknowledge method 'only fits mathematical reasoning' and requires modifications for coding, limiting applicability

Missing reproducibility details: no code availability, answer extraction strategy unspecified (Algorithm 1), prompt engineering is ad-hoc and task-specific, training data subset selection not rigorously justified
Insufficient ablation studies: no systematic investigation of hint quality, type importance, or contribution of individual components beyond descriptive analysis

strengths: Clear problem formulation of exploration stagnation with formal analysis
Practical approach that avoids external guidance (human annotations or stronger models)
Comprehensive analysis of training dynamics showing reduced unsolved samples while maintaining exploration
Thorough empirical evaluation across six benchmarks with ablations (with/without entropy loss)
Theoretical framework attempting to justify state-space pruning mechanism
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core mechanism (retry with incorrect answers as hints) is intuitive but incremental; conceptually similar to EvoCoT with unclear distinction
Weak experimental validation on larger models: only 4B and 8B models tested; no experiments on 13B+ models despite computational feasibility being critical for RLVR claims
Tiny training datasets (9,189 samples for 4B, 3,236 for 8B) and very short training (300 steps); authors acknowledge 8B underperformance is due to dataset size
Inconsistent 8B results: Pass@1 improvement is only +0.07 without entropy loss and +1.73 with it—far less convincing than 4B claims

Confounded experimental design: LTE uses 2× rollouts (16 vs 8) on none-pass samples, making it unclear whether improvements come from hints or simply more data; vanilla extra rollouts baseline is weak

Questionable methodological choices: (1) setting old policy probability to 1 in importance sampling 'for computational efficiency' violates proper IS correction; (2) treating all truncated responses as invalid is crude; (3) three-way prompt classification appears ad-hoc
Weak theoretical contribution: Eq. (15) assumes δ>0 without empirical verification; information gain analysis (A.3) is trivial; framework borrowed from CoT-Space (Gan et al., 2025)

Narrow scope: method is mathematics-specific requiring concise verifiable answers; acknowledged applicability to coding/other tasks is unclear; design choices (e.g., 'think concisely') are domain-specific
Inconsistent naming: contributions section mentions 'SeltHint' while method is called 'LTE' throughout, creating confusion
Missing critical ablations: no analysis of which hint templates help most; no error analysis of when method fails or hints mislead; no computational cost accounting despite 2× rollouts
Missing strong baselines: no direct comparison with EvoCoT or other recent guidance-free methods mentioned in related work

strengths: Clear problem formulation of exploration stagnation with formal mathematical analysis showing zero gradients for none-pass samples
Practical approach requiring no external expert guidance, addressing a real limitation of existing RLVR methods
Strong empirical results on Qwen3-4B-Base (+6.38 Pass@1, +9.00 Pass@k) with consistent improvements across six mathematics benchmarks
Comprehensive experimental analysis including training dynamics, entropy tracking, response length evolution, and none-pass sample reduction
Proper off-policy handling through mixed-policy optimization with regularized importance sampling
Thorough evaluation with both Pass@1 and Pass@k metrics, with/without entropy loss, on two model sizes
Well-organized presentation with clear algorithm description and informative visualizations
weaknesses: Critical limitation: method evaluated only on mathematical reasoning tasks despite being presented as general RLVR improvement; acknowledged need for modifications for other tasks (coding, QA)
Small model scale: experiments limited to 4B and 8B models; paper acknowledges lack of larger-scale testing and unclear applicability to flagship models
Inconsistent results on 8B model: significantly weaker improvements than 4B (+0.89 average without entropy loss), attributed to small training data, raising robustness concerns
Limited novelty: core idea of using incorrect answers as prompts is straightforward and incremental; mixed-policy optimization heavily borrows from concurrent work
Missing critical ablations: no systematic study of hint type selection, number of incorrect answers included, or regularization parameter γ sensitivity
Off-policy approximation: treating old policy term as 1 lacks impact analysis and is justified only by computational convenience, not theoretical soundness
Weak theoretical contributions: assumptions (α ∼ Ω(1)) lack empirical validation; information gain argument too high-level; relies entirely on existing CoT-Space framework
No experimental comparison with related methods (EvoCoT, Dou et al., Chen et al.) addressing similar exploration problems
Evaluation protocol concerns: Pass@k improvements measured on validation set during training, not true test-time; unclear practical deployment benefits
Lack of statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests despite high variance across benchmarks
Hint design concerns: truncation-based categorization is ad-hoc; informal instruction 'do not mention hint explicitly' lacks validation of actual model behavior
Missing reproducibility details: no computational cost comparison with baselines; training convergence not verified; no code availability mentioned

strengths: Clear problem formulation: Exploration stagnation in RLVR is well-motivated with formal mathematical analysis (Eq. 5) explaining why standard GRPO fails on none-pass samples.
Intuitive and practical approach: Using the model's own incorrect answers as hints is elegant, requires no external resources, and is well-justified analogically.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Consistent results across two model sizes, six benchmarks, multiple baselines, both Pass@1 and Pass@k metrics, with detailed ablation and training dynamics analysis.
Thorough empirical analysis: Figure 4 documents reduction in none-pass samples over training; Figure 5 provides convincing evidence of maintained exploration while improving exploitation.
Strong reproducibility foundation: Clear algorithm, detailed hyperparameters, implementation details, and promised code release support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: The contribution is primarily a combination of existing techniques (hinted rollouts, extra rollouts, mixed-policy optimization). Each component is borrowed from prior work, making the core novelty incremental.

Severely restricted scope: Only evaluated on mathematical reasoning despite general framing. Acknowledged limitation to tasks with 'concise answer formats' eliminates coding, open-ended reasoning, and most NLP tasks. Model evaluation limited to Qwen3 family only.

Unfair baseline comparisons: Authors obtained poor results for ReLIFT and EvoCoT using exact official scripts, undermining comparison validity. More critically, basic LTE achieves only +5 Pass@1 over GRPO, while LTE† (with entropy loss) gains only +2.4 over LUFFY—suggesting core hinting contribution is modest without entropy control.

Problematic off-policy treatment: The approximation of π_θold(o'_i,t | Hq, q, o_i,<t) = 1 in Eq. 6 'for computational efficiency' lacks justification and potentially ignores important distribution mismatch between hinted and normal prompts, conflating importance sampling with behavior cloning.

Weak theoretical analysis: The theoretical framework (Appendix A) relies on unproven assumptions (δ > 0, α > Ω(1/n)) and is loosely connected to the actual hinting strategy. Does not validate that prompt-based hints achieve the claimed state space pruning.
Missing statistical rigor: No error bars, multiple runs, or significance tests despite inherent noise in reasoning tasks. Single-run results are insufficient for empirical claims.

Unexplained design choices: (1) Random replacement strategy in mixed-policy optimization lacks justification; (2) Treating all truncated responses as invalid may discard extractable answers; (3) No sensitivity analysis on brittle prompt engineering choices.
Incomplete failure analysis: No investigation of when hints are misleading or harmful, or systematic study of prompt template sensitivity which could affect reproducibility.

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine limitation of on-policy RLVR (exploration stagnation) where models cannot solve problems beyond initial capability
Practical approach using only model's own failures as guidance, avoiding dependency on external models or human annotations
Comprehensive empirical analysis across 6 benchmarks and 2 model sizes with both Pass@1 and Pass@k metrics; detailed visualization of training dynamics
Clear demonstration that LTE reduces none-pass samples during training and maintains higher entropy, providing evidence for addressing exploration stagnation
Ablation studies validating contribution of both hint types, with both components shown to be necessary
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core idea of using model failures as hints for extra rollouts is incremental; hints in RLVR already explored by prior work (EvoCoT, ReLIFT, LUFFY)

Severely narrow scope: only evaluated on mathematical reasoning; authors acknowledge method 'only fits mathematical reasoning due to concise format of answers' and cannot extend to coding or other reasoning tasks, limiting impact for general NLP venue

Weak theoretical analysis in Appendix A: assumes (Eq. 15) what should be proven (δ > 0); final result (Eq. 21) is tautological given unjustified assumptions; provides post-hoc rationalization without actionable insights

Serious experimental fairness concerns: (1) admitted compatibility issues with ReLIFT and EvoCoT baseline implementations without proper investigation; (2) LTE vs LTE† conflates entropy loss with hints, making attribution unclear; (3) modest improvement over GRPOExtra (+7.29/+10.04) lacks statistical significance testing and confidence intervals

Broken importance sampling: Eq. (6) simplification setting π_θ_old term to 1 for 'efficiency' violates importance sampling framework without theoretical justification, potentially introducing systematic bias

Ad-hoc design choices: three different prompt templates for truncation cases with instruction 'don't mention hints' appear hand-crafted; response length increases significantly (Fig. 5d), contradicting efficiency claims and inflating computational cost
Insufficient error analysis: no investigation of failure modes, when hints hurt, what mistakes are prevented, or whether model truly learns to avoid errors vs. being steered toward answers
Reproducibility barriers: code unavailable for review; answer extraction method unspecified; 6-9 day training requirement on expensive hardware; no hyperparameter sensitivity analysis

strengths: Clear problem motivation with formal characterization of exploration stagnation (Eq. 5); the core issue is compelling and well-articulated
Simple, practical, and intuitive solution requiring no external expert guidance, unlike methods depending on ground truth or stronger LM outputs
Strong empirical results: LTE outperforms GRPO by +4.94 (Pass@1) and +7.30 (Pass@k); LTE† achieves +2.41/+2.15 over LUFFY without external solutions

Thorough experimental analysis demonstrating mitigation of exploration stagnation: none-pass samples consistently decrease (Figure 4a) while some-pass samples remain high (Figure 4b), directly validating the core claim
Comprehensive evaluation across six diverse mathematical benchmarks and two model sizes with both Pass@1 and Pass@k metrics; consistent improvements across settings
Well-designed ablation study (Table 3) confirms both hint components contribute meaningfully; analysis of training dynamics (Figure 5) shows continued improvement vs. baseline stagnation
Theoretical grounding in CoT-Space framework (Appendix A) with state-space pruning analysis connecting intuition to formal reasoning
Excellent reproducibility: code availability promised, detailed hyperparameters, clear algorithm description, implementation details provided
weaknesses: Severely limited domain scope—only mathematical reasoning evaluated despite positioning as solution to general RLVR problem; method relies on concise answer formats with no evidence of transferability to coding, QA, or other domains (acknowledged limitation with no path forward)

Comparison fairness concerns: authors report poor results for ReLIFT and EvoCoT with attribution to 'compatibility of foundation models' but provide no investigation; undermines confidence in relative rankings and makes it difficult to assess true comparative advantage

Contribution attribution unclear: strongest results (LTE†) include entropy loss added for 'fair comparison'; without entropy loss, improvements over GRPOExtra are modest (~5 points); degree to which entropy loss vs. trial-and-error mechanism drives improvements not isolated

Design choices lack justification: categorical treatment of all-truncated/some-truncated/none-truncated samples is somewhat ad-hoc; treating all truncated responses as failures ignores potentially extractable answers; γ=0.1 borrowed from LUFFY without justification

Theoretical analysis relies on strong assumptions (Eqs. 15-16) about instruction-following capability and assumption α > Ω(1/n) lacks rigorous justification; gap between theoretical result and practical improvements remains

Experimental limitations: training only 500 steps (convergence unclear from figures); maximum response length 8,192 acknowledged as restrictive; only 4B/8B models tested with no evidence of scaling; no significance testing or error bars; evaluation uses small k values

Limited novelty: learning from failures is established in RL; using hints in RLVR known from prior work (EvoCoT, LUFFY); main novelty (model's own mistakes) is somewhat incremental; mixed-policy optimization adapted from LUFFY

Missing critical analyses: no investigation of failure modes or when hints mislead the model; no comparison with simpler alternatives (negative example training, data augmentation); impact of treating old policy as 1 in importance sampling not analyzed; no solution quality analysis beyond correctness
